sub: BPH grows in the transition zone and cancer in the peripheral zone; the tunica albuginea explains Peyronie disease, fracture and priapism, and HPV drives penile cancer.

pretest.q: In which zone of the prostate does benign prostatic hyperplasia arise?
pretest.why: BPH is hyperplasia of glands and stroma in the transition zone, which surrounds the urethra, so it obstructs urine flow early. The peripheral zone at the back is where most cancers arise.

w.Peripheral zone: This zone forms about 70% of the gland and lies against the rectum; most adenocarcinomas arise here and can be felt as a hard nodule, but it does not squeeze the urethra.
w.Central zone: The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts at the base of the gland and is rarely diseased, so neither hyperplasia nor cancer usually begins there.
w.Anterior fibromuscular stroma: This anterior band contains muscle and fibrous tissue but no glands, so it cannot give rise to glandular hyperplasia or adenocarcinoma.

pretest.q: Which biopsy finding most strongly favors prostate adenocarcinoma over benign glands?
pretest.why: Benign prostate glands keep a layer of basal cells that stains with p63. Cancer glands lose it, and they are small, crowded and lined by one cell layer with prominent nucleoli.

w.Corpora amylacea: These laminated concretions accumulate in the lumens of benign glands in older men, so finding them argues for normal or hyperplastic tissue rather than cancer.
w.Papillary infoldings: Papillary infolding of the epithelium is a normal architectural feature of benign prostate glands and of hyperplasia, not a sign of malignancy.
w.Two-cell lining: Normal glands have a basal layer beneath the secretory layer, so a two-cell lining is the benign pattern; malignant glands have only one layer.

pretest.q: Which drug class lowers the measured PSA by about half within months?
pretest.why: Finasteride and dutasteride block DHT formation, shrink the gland and lower PSA about 50%, so the measured value is doubled when screening for cancer.

w.Alpha-1 blockers: Tamsulosin and similar drugs relax smooth muscle to improve flow but do not shrink epithelium, so they leave the PSA level unchanged.
w.PDE5 inhibitors: Tadalafil raises cGMP in smooth muscle to ease urinary symptoms and erections, and it has no effect on prostate epithelial secretion of PSA.
w.Antimuscarinic drugs: These relax the detrusor to reduce urgency and have no action on prostate tissue, so serum PSA does not change with them.

body: Which zone of the prostate gets which disease?

The prostate is a walnut-sized gland that wraps around the urethra just below the bladder, and its zones decide which disease appears. The {{rp21_tz|transition zone}} hugs the urethra, so overgrowth there squeezes it early; this is **benign prostatic hyperplasia** (BPH). The {{rp21_pz|peripheral zone}} is about 70% of the gland and lies at the back against the rectum, so a hard nodule there is felt on a digital rectal exam, and it gives rise to 70 to 80% of cancers. The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely diseased, and the anterior fibromuscular stroma has no glands. Normal glands are tubuloalveolar with papillary infoldings and a two-cell lining, and older men show laminated concretions called **corpora amylacea**; the seminal vesicle looks similar but is highly folded and has none.
What drives BPH, and which drug treats which part?

BPH is true **hyperplasia**: both gland cells and stromal cells multiply. Testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase type 2 into {{rp21_dht|dihydrotestosterone}} (DHT), which binds the androgen receptor more tightly and drives the growth, so men castrated before puberty or born without the enzyme never develop BPH. Nodules can raise the gland to 100 g. As the urethra narrows, lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) appear: weak stream, hesitancy and incomplete emptying, plus frequency, urgency and nocturia. The bladder wall thickens and then fails, so retention, infections, stones and bilateral hydronephrosis can follow. BPH is not premalignant, and size does not predict cancer.

BPH obstructs in two ways. The static part is the bulk of the overgrown tissue, which **5-alpha-reductase inhibitors** (finasteride, dutasteride) shrink over months by blocking DHT formation. The dynamic part is smooth-muscle tone in the stroma, capsule and bladder neck, which **alpha-1 blockers** relax within days. Tamsulosin and silodosin are alpha-1A selective, whereas terazosin and doxazosin are nonselective and also lower blood pressure. Daily tadalafil treats LUTS and erectile dysfunction together. When drugs fail, transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) removes transition zone tissue, which treats BPH but not peripheral zone cancer.
Retrograde or absent ejaculation; floppy iris syndrome at cataract surgery
Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia; PSA halves; teratogenic to handle
Bulk gets a 5-ARI, tone gets an alpha-blocker

Size correlates poorly with symptoms, because a 30 g gland with high muscle tone can obstruct more than a 90 g gland. An alpha-blocker works in days and is the usual first drug. A **5-alpha-reductase inhibitor** takes months and helps most when the gland is large, and the two together slow progression best.
What causes prostatitis, and what should be avoided?

Prostatitis has four patterns. **Acute bacterial prostatitis** causes fever, dysuria and a very tender, swollen, boggy prostate; E. coli is the usual cause, and in sexually active young men Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are common. Vigorous massage is avoided because it can push bacteria into the blood. **Chronic bacterial prostatitis** appears as recurrent urinary infections with the same organism, because antibiotics reach the gland poorly and it acts as a reservoir. **Chronic pelvic pain syndrome**, with pain and negative cultures, is the most common type, and repeated antibiotics do not help it. Granulomatous prostatitis, often after BCG for bladder cancer, feels hard and can mimic cancer.
Who gets prostate cancer, and how is it recognized?

Prostate adenocarcinoma is the most common cancer in men. Risk rises with age, is higher in men of African ancestry, and doubles with an affected first-degree relative, so a family history matters; germline **BRCA2** mutations predict aggressive disease. Most tumors are multifocal in the peripheral zone and silent, so a raised {{rp21_psa|PSA}} and needle biopsy find them. The cells form small, crowded glands with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli and perineural invasion. The key criterion is loss of the {{rp21_basal|basal cell layer}}: p63 and keratin stains are negative, while AMACR is positive. The Gleason grade, which scores gland architecture, is grouped into Grade Groups 1 to 5.

PSA is a protease that liquefies semen, so it is **organ-specific, not cancer-specific**: BPH, prostatitis, urinary retention, instrumentation and ejaculation raise it, while 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors halve it, so the value is doubled. A low free-to-total PSA ratio favors cancer. Because screening finds many slow tumors, it is a shared decision. Autopsy studies show **latent** cancers in many older men, but only a **clinically significant** cancer, usually Gleason 7 or higher, needs treatment; treating the rest is overdiagnosis. Advanced cancer reaches the lumbar spine and pelvis through the Batson venous plexus as osteoblastic metastases, with a raised alkaline phosphatase.
Why does leuprolide first raise testosterone before it lowers it?

Leuprolide is a GnRH agonist, so at first it stimulates the pituitary receptor just as natural GnRH does, and LH and testosterone surge for one to two weeks. In advanced cancer this flare can worsen bone pain or urinary obstruction. Natural GnRH arrives in pulses, and the receptor needs the pauses to recover. A continuous signal makes the gonadotrophs downregulate the receptor, so LH release collapses and testosterone falls to castrate levels within weeks. An antiandrogen such as bicalutamide, started first, blocks the flare at the androgen receptor, and the antagonist degarelix has no flare.
Building androgen deprivation therapy in order
A GnRH agonist (leuprolide, goserelin) with an antiandrogen to cover the flare, or the antagonist degarelix, which works at once.
Block the receptor or the synthesis

Bicalutamide, flutamide (hepatotoxic) and enzalutamide block the androgen receptor. Abiraterone inhibits CYP17A1; cortisol falls, ACTH rises and mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia) follows unless prednisone is added.
Hot flashes, lost libido and erections, gynecomastia, fatigue and bone loss; check bone density and give calcium, vitamin D and an antiresorptive drug if fracture risk is high.
What goes wrong with the foreskin, glans and urethral opening?

**Phimosis** is a foreskin that cannot be pulled back. It is normal in boys until about age 3 to 5, but pathologic with lichen sclerosus, recurrent balanitis or diabetes, and then topical steroids or circumcision are used. **Paraphimosis** is a retracted foreskin that cannot be brought forward; venous congestion and edema threaten the arterial supply, so it is an emergency, often caused by not replacing the foreskin after a catheter. Hypospadias, a ventral urethral opening, comes from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds and travels with cryptorchidism; repair is at 6 to 18 months, and circumcision waits because the foreskin is used. Epispadias is a dorsal opening, often with bladder exstrophy.
Red itchy glans, satellite papules; diabetes

The {{rp21_ta|tunica albuginea}} is the inelastic sheath around the corpora cavernosa. In **Peyronie disease**, repeated microtrauma causes bleeding under it and abnormal scarring, so a fibrous plaque forms that does not stretch. The erect penis shows painful curvature toward the plaque, with shortening and sometimes erectile dysfunction from venous leak. It is a fibromatosis that travels with Dupuytren contracture and plantar fibromatosis, and injections or surgery wait for the stable phase. In **penile fracture**, the thinned tunica of an erect penis ruptures with a pop, sudden detumescence and an eggplant-shaped hematoma; urethral injury occurs in 10 to 20%, so repair is urgent.
Sickle cell disease, trazodone, cocaine, PDE5 inhibitors, injections
Ischemic priapism is a urologic emergency

An erection lasting over 4 hours with pain means blood is trapped in the corpora, which turns acidotic and hypoxic, and fibrosis starts within 24 to 48 hours, ending in erectile dysfunction. Treat at once by aspiration, phenylephrine injection or a shunt; painless **nonischemic** priapism after perineal trauma is not an emergency.
How does penile squamous neoplasia progress?

Condyloma acuminata, caused by low-risk HPV 6 and 11, forms warts with koilocytes and rarely progresses. Premalignant lesions come from high-risk HPV 16 and 18 and show full-thickness atypia above an intact basement membrane: **Bowen disease** on the shaft, **erythroplasia of Queyrat**, a red velvety plaque on the glans, and bowenoid papulosis, small papules in young men that usually regress. About 10% of penile intraepithelial neoplasia becomes **squamous cell carcinoma**, 95% of penile cancers; risks are HPV 16 and 18, lack of circumcision, phimosis, lichen sclerosus and smoking. Penile lymph drains to inguinal nodes, so groin nodes set the prognosis, whereas the testis drains to para-aortic nodes.

body.q: A 68-year-old man has a weak stream and nocturia, and a smooth, symmetric, enlarged prostate. Which reasoning best explains why his gland obstructs the urethra yet is probably benign?
o: The overgrowth is in the peripheral zone, which compresses the urethra from behind, while cancer usually arises around the urethra
A smooth gland proves the enlargement is infectious, because prostatitis always produces a symmetric gland with fever
The overgrowth is in the transition zone, which surrounds the urethra, while cancer usually arises in the peripheral zone at the back
Hypertrophy of existing cells, not hyperplasia, is responsible, so the gland cannot contain malignant cells
body.why: BPH is hyperplasia of glands and stroma in the transition zone, the tissue that wraps the urethra, so even modest growth narrows it and causes a weak stream and nocturia. Prostate cancer usually starts in the peripheral zone, far from the urethra, where it grows silently and often feels like a hard nodule rather than a smooth gland. A smooth, symmetric, enlarged gland with obstructive symptoms therefore points to BPH, and a mild PSA rise fits BPH too, because PSA is organ-specific rather than cancer-specific.

grid.q: Which of these fit benign prostatic hyperplasia rather than prostate cancer?
items: Smooth symmetric gland on rectal exam
